meta.title: Who really said "I learned long ago never to wrestle with a pig. You get dirty, and besides, the pig likes it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. Shaw never said it. This is an anonymous folk adage popularized by mediator Cyrus Ching in 1948; Shaw wasn't credited until a 1994 Usenet post.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I learned long ago never to wrestle with a pig. You get dirty, and besides, the pig likes it'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous folk saying, popularized by labor mediator Cyrus Ching in 1948. George Bernard Shaw wasn't credited until 1994 — with zero evidence.

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — an anonymous folk adage
answer.authorDates: Adage evolved c. 1872–1948 · brought to prominence 1948
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence George Bernard Shaw ever said or wrote this. Quote Investigator ↗ shows the saying evolved anonymously over decades — a partial “hog” version appeared by 1872, and the memorable telling was popularized by U.S. labor mediator Cyrus Stuart Ching in a 1948 profile, where he credited an unnamed uncle. Shaw wasn’t linked to it until a 1994 Usenet post, 44 years after his death.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Cyrus Stuart Ching, Saturday Evening Post profile, 1948
1994 Usenet post — 44 years after Shaw's death

source.excerpt: He said, ‘What’s the sense of wrestling with a pig? You both get all over muddy… and the pig likes it.’
trail: A partial precursor using “hog” appears in an 1872 letter by J. Frank Condon: “he who wrestles with a hog must expect to be spattered with filth,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
The memorable “and the pig likes it” telling was popularized by labor mediator Cyrus Stuart Ching in a 1948 Saturday Evening Post profile ↗, where he credited an unnamed uncle.
Quote Investigator ↗ concludes: the adage is anonymous, and the ascriptions to George Bernard Shaw, Mark Twain, and Abraham Lincoln are unsupported.
Shaw was first credited only in a 1994 Usenet message ↗, decades after his 1950 death.
source.excerptNote: Cyrus Ching’s 1948 telling, crediting an unnamed uncle — the version Quote Investigator identifies as the key popularization. The polished “I learned long ago…” wording credited to Shaw appears only in later, undocumented retellings.

source.rightsNote: This is an anonymous folk adage with no single identifiable author or first-publication work; the polished wording credited to Shaw cannot be tied to any documented source. Because the wording’s origin is unknown, no copyright status is asserted. (Ching’s 1948 telling is a distinct, differently worded version.)

author.name: Cyrus Stuart Ching
author.heading: The man who actually made it famous
author.metaLine: 1876–1967 · U.S. labor mediator · first head of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service
author.bio: Cyrus Stuart Ching was a towering (6’7”) American industrial-relations expert who became the first director of the U.S. Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service in 1947. In a widely read 1948 Saturday Evening Post profile he told the pig story — but explicitly credited it to an unnamed uncle, never claiming it as his own. He is the great popularizer of the modern wording, not its author; the saying itself is anonymous folk wisdom.

misattribution.heading: A magnet-name misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “quotation superstar” misattribution: a punchy anonymous adage pinned onto famous names long after their deaths. Quote Investigator found no evidence any of them said it.

items.why: Shaw (1856–1950) was first credited only in a 1994 Usenet post ↗ — 44 years after he died — with no record in any of his plays, letters, or prefaces.
Twain was credited via a 2001 Usenet message ↗, with no supporting evidence, per Quote Investigator.
Lincoln was tentatively credited in a 1996 Usenet message ↗ — even the poster questioned the attribution.

misattribution.truthLine: The truth: an anonymous adage that evolved over decades and was popularized by mediator Cyrus S. Ching in 1948 — not Shaw, Twain, or Lincoln ↗.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Shaw
lead: The line is a perfect “quotation superstar” magnet: witty, worldly, and faintly cynical — exactly the register readers associate with George Bernard Shaw. That plausibility is precisely why it drifted onto his name in the internet era, with no source behind it.

The real history is more democratic. As Quote Investigator documents, the saying was folk wisdom that sharpened over generations of retelling, its final comic beat — that the pig enjoys the fight — crystallizing by the 1940s and reaching a national audience through a genial labor mediator, not a celebrated playwright.
context.pull: Witty, cynical, quotable — so it drifted onto Shaw. But the paper trail leads to an anonymous uncle and a 1948 magazine profile.
